Toward a Multidimensional CDI-CAT: Noun/Predicate Lexical Category Bias

George Kachergis

2026-09-16

Motivation

The existing Japanese CDI-CAT (adaptive_cdi_production.Rmd) estimates a single, unidimensional production-vocabulary ability. A collaborator (Hiromichi Hagihara, Osaka University) is interested in a companion measure of lexical category bias: whether a child’s vocabulary leans toward nouns or toward predicates (verbs and adjectives), relative to what would be expected from their overall vocabulary size. This is motivated by Hagihara, Tan, & Frank’s submitted cross-linguistic paper (“Lexical category biases in children’s early vocabulary”), which finds systematic, cross-linguistically variable noun/verb/adjective biases, and specifically notes that many resources (including, by default, Wordbank’s own lexical_category coding) collapse verbs and adjectives into a single “predicates” class for languages – Japanese among them – where adjectives conjugate like verbs.

This document summarizes the pipeline built to support a multidimensional CAT that adaptively estimates general vocabulary ability and a noun-vs-predicate bias score, from data prep through a first CAT simulation. Scripts referenced below live in multidim/01 through multidim/05; this document does not refit any models – it loads their saved output.

items <- read_csv(here("multidim/item_lexical_categories.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
efa_loadings <- read_csv(here("multidim/efa2_loadings.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
bifactor_items <- read_csv(here("multidim/bifactor_item_params.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
bifactor_scores <- read_csv(here("multidim/bifactor_scores.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
cat_summary_wrule <- read_csv(here("multidim/cat_simulation_summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(criteria = "Wrule")
criteria_comparison <- read_csv(here("multidim/criteria_comparison_full_sample.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
resp_data <- readRDS(here("multidim/noun_predicate_response_data.Rds"))
sim_results_drule <- readRDS(here("multidim/cat_simulation_results_drule.Rds"))

1. Item classification

All 711 production-vocabulary items are classified into nouns, verbs, adjectives, function_words, or other from their CDI semantic category (category_en), following the same category → class mapping Wordbank uses for Japanese (verified directly against wordbankr::get_item_data(language = "Japanese", form = "WS")$lexical_category, which folds verbs and adjectives into “predicates”). The pos2 column collapses verbs+adjectives into predicate, which is the 2-dimensional split used for the CAT below.

items %>%
  count(lexical_class, pos2) %>%
  arrange(pos2) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Lexical class", "CAT dimension (pos2)", "N items"),
        caption = "Item counts by lexical class and by the 2-dimensional CAT grouping.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Item counts by lexical class and by the 2-dimensional CAT grouping.
Lexical class CAT dimension (pos2) N items
noun noun 312
function_word other 81
other other 152
adjective predicate 63
verb predicate 103

The item bank used for the multidimensional model is the 478 noun + predicate items (312 nouns, 166 predicates = 103 verbs + 63 adjectives); function words and the residual “other” category (233 items) are excluded, since neither should carry a noun/predicate-specific signal.

2. Sample

The response data are the same combined WG+WS production dataset and exclusion criteria used for the existing unidimensional CAT (adaptive_cdi_production.Rmd): administrations from children <12 or >38 months, non-producers ≥12 months, and children at ceiling are dropped, leaving 939 administrations (639 WS, 300 WG). 12.6% of noun/predicate item responses were missing (mostly WS-only items on WG-form administrations) and were imputed from each child’s fitted bifactor scores (mirt::imputeMissing()) before running the CAT simulation.

3. Exploratory factor check

Before committing to a confirmatory structure, an exploratory 2-factor IRT model (mirt, oblimin rotation) was fit to the 478-item noun+predicate matrix, as a check on whether the a priori noun/predicate split is empirically recoverable.

ggplot(efa_loadings, aes(x = F1, y = F2, color = pos2)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "F1 (general)", y = "F2 (noun vs. predicate)", color = "Item type",
       title = "Exploratory 2-factor loadings") +
  theme_bw()

efa_loadings %>%
  filter(pos2 %in% c("noun", "predicate")) %>%
  group_by(pos2) %>%
  summarise(mean_F1 = mean(F1), mean_F2 = mean(F2), n = n()) %>%
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Mean rotated loadings by item type.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Mean rotated loadings by item type.
pos2 mean_F1 mean_F2 n
noun 0.865 -0.101 312
predicate 0.887 0.163 166

Every item’s dominant loading is on F1 (range 0.55-0.96) – a general vocabulary factor, exactly as expected given raw noun/predicate production proportions correlate r=.94 with each other and r > .97 with total vocabulary size (the “availability problem” the source paper explicitly warns about: raw category proportions are mostly just overall vocabulary size in disguise). F2 is a real but much smaller factor: predicate items load positively (mean 0.163) and noun items negatively (mean -0.101), a highly reliable separation (Welch t = -32.8, p < .0001), and F1/F2 came out nearly orthogonal after rotation (r = -0.015) without being constrained to be. This is exactly the signature of a bifactor structure – one dominant general factor plus a much smaller, genuinely separable specific factor – so that was fit next as the confirmatory model.

4. Confirmatory bifactor model

mirt::bfactor() was fit with every item loading on a general factor (G) plus one of two orthogonal specific factors: S1 (nouns only) or S2 (predicates only). The bias measure of interest is S1 - S2 per child.

bifactor_items %>%
  mutate(own_specific = if_else(pos2 == "noun", S1_noun, S2_predicate)) %>%
  group_by(pos2) %>%
  summarise(mean_G = mean(G), mean_own_specific = mean(own_specific), n = n()) %>%
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Mean general (G) and own-specific-factor loadings by item type.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Mean general (G) and own-specific-factor loadings by item type.
pos2 mean_G mean_own_specific n
noun 5.33 1.20 312
predicate 5.88 1.72 166 
rel <- empirical_rxx(bifactor_scores %>% select(G, S1_noun, S2_predicate, SE_G, SE_S1_noun, SE_S2_predicate) %>%
                        as.matrix())
tibble(dimension = names(rel), empirical_rxx = rel) %>%
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Empirical reliability of full-item-bank (non-adaptive) factor scores.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Empirical reliability of full-item-bank (non-adaptive) factor scores.
dimension empirical_rxx
G 0.93
S1_noun 0.71
S2_predicate 0.64

The key validation: does the bias score actually separate from general vocabulary size, unlike the raw proportions?

bifactor_scores <- bifactor_scores %>% mutate(noun_predicate_bias = S1_noun - S2_predicate)

ggplot(bifactor_scores, aes(x = production, y = noun_predicate_bias)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Total production (sum score)", y = "Noun/predicate bias (S1 - S2)",
       title = sprintf("r = %.2f", cor(bifactor_scores$production, bifactor_scores$noun_predicate_bias))) +
  theme_bw()

Raw noun/predicate proportions correlated r ≈ .94-.99 with total vocabulary size; the bifactor bias score correlates only r = -0.16 with production and r = -0.17 with age – confirming the specific factor is capturing a residual tilt, not just vocabulary size in disguise.

One caveat: although S1 and S2 are constrained to be latently orthogonal in the model, their EAP score estimates still correlate r = 0.48 – a known bifactor artifact (shared estimation noise across items), which means the practical precision of the bias difference score is worse than either specific factor’s own reliability suggests.

5. CAT simulation

5.1 Item selection criterion: Drule vs. Wrule

Two multidimensional item-selection criteria were compared: Drule (maximizes the determinant of the full 3-D information matrix) and Wrule with weights c(0,1,1) (explicitly down-weights G, on the hypothesis that the specific factors would otherwise be starved of items since G’s loadings are 3-5x larger). That hypothesis turned out to be wrong:

criteria_comparison %>%
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Drule vs. Wrule, full N=939 sample, matched max_items ceilings.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Drule vs. Wrule, full N=939 sample, matched max_items ceilings.
criteria max_items mean_n_items mean_SE_G mean_SE_S1 mean_SE_S2 r_bias_vs_full r_G_vs_full
Drule 100 75.241 0.208 0.639 0.629 0.932 0.989
Wrule 100 98.027 0.224 0.652 0.660 0.929 0.983
Drule 200 131.185 0.204 0.631 0.621 0.947 0.990
Wrule 200 161.583 0.212 0.627 0.629 0.967 0.987

Drule reaches comparable-or-better specific-factor precision using noticeably fewer items on average than Wrule at the same ceiling – once G is well-estimated, conditioning on it is what actually helps resolve S1/S2, so items chosen for general informativeness end up serving the bias dimensions better than items chosen to deliberately avoid G. Drule is used from here on.

5.2 Achievable precision ceiling

Even a full, non-adaptive 478-item administration only reaches a fairly modest specific-factor precision (Section 4’s reliability table: SE ≈ 0.5 for S1/S2, vs. ≈ 0.17 for G) – substantially worse than can be reached for general ability, and worse than the min_SEM = 0.3 target used for G in the existing unidimensional CAT. The CAT simulation below uses min_SEM = c(0.3, 0.5, 0.5), grounded in that ceiling, rather than an arbitrary tighter target the bias dimensions could never reach.

5.3 Simulation results (Drule, full N = 939 sample)

criteria_comparison %>%
  filter(criteria == "Drule") %>%
  bind_rows(cat_summary_wrule %>% filter(max_items == 50) %>%
              transmute(criteria, max_items, mean_n_items, mean_SE_G = mean_SE_G,
                        mean_SE_S1 = mean_SE_S1, mean_SE_S2 = mean_SE_S2,
                        r_bias_vs_full = r_bias_vs_full, r_G_vs_full = r_G_vs_full)) %>%
  arrange(max_items) %>%
  kable(digits = 3,
        caption = "CAT simulation results: item budget vs. recovered precision and agreement with the full-item-bank estimate.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
CAT simulation results: item budget vs. recovered precision and agreement with the full-item-bank estimate.
criteria max_items mean_n_items mean_SE_G mean_SE_S1 mean_SE_S2 r_bias_vs_full r_G_vs_full
Wrule 50 50.000 0.260 0.720 0.735 0.866 0.968
Drule 100 75.241 0.208 0.639 0.629 0.932 0.989
Drule 200 131.185 0.204 0.631 0.621 0.947 0.990 
d_demo <- resp_data$d_demo
p100 <- sim_results_drule[["100"]]$parms
p100$data_id <- d_demo$data_id
p100 <- left_join(p100, bifactor_scores %>% select(data_id, bias_full = noun_predicate_bias), by = "data_id")

ggplot(p100, aes(x = bias_full, y = bias_cat)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Full-item-bank bias (S1 - S2)", y = "CAT-estimated bias (max 100 items, Drule)",
       title = sprintf("r = %.2f, mean %.0f items administered", cor(p100$bias_cat, p100$bias_full), mean(p100$n_items))) +
  theme_bw()

With a 100-item ceiling, Drule administers 75 items on average and recovers the bias score at r = .93 against the full 478-item estimate; extending the ceiling to 200 items (131 administered on average) reaches r = .95. For comparison, the existing unidimensional production CAT gets away with ~25-50 items total because it only has to resolve one dimension – the bias dimension is intrinsically harder to measure precisely, so a noun/predicate-bias CAT will need a substantially larger item budget than the existing vocabulary-size CAT to reach comparable fidelity.

6. Summary and open questions

  • Item bank: 478 items (312 noun, 166 predicate) reliably classified from existing CDI category metadata – no new item coding was needed.
  • Model: a bifactor structure (general vocabulary factor + orthogonal noun-specific and predicate-specific factors) is empirically supported (the EFA check found a dominant general factor plus a small, real, near-orthogonal secondary noun/predicate split) and successfully decouples the bias score from vocabulary size/age (r ≈ -.16, down from r ≈ .94-.99 for raw proportions).
  • CAT: Drule item selection with min_SEM = c(0.3, 0.5, 0.5); a ~100-item budget recovers the bias estimate at r = .93 vs. the full item bank, ~200 items reaches r = .95.

Open questions worth settling with Hiromichi before further development:

  1. Deployment stopping rule: fixed item count (~100-150) vs. adaptive SE-based stopping – the latter is principled but a meaningful fraction of children will still hit the item ceiling given the precision ceiling in Section 5.2.
  2. 3-way split: whether to pursue nouns/verbs/adjectives as three specific factors instead of the 2-way noun/predicate collapse used here (the source paper’s own adjective bias was the noisiest and least typologically predictable of the three categories, so a 3-way model may need more items per dimension than are available, but it would match the paper’s own finer-grained distinction).
  3. Whether a shorter, purpose-built noun/predicate-only CAT (this document) should be a standalone instrument, or whether it’s preferable to fold these dimensions into a single administration alongside the existing production CAT (sharing items, one longer adaptive session instead of two).
